play C/kid.verdict: From the 10-year-old's seat: the payoff is great and everything around it is unreadable. When a Conductor shatter lands, 100-211 hp vanishes in one hit and robots or the boss pop. That is the surprise that keeps a kid playing. But the kid did nothing to earn it. In `lens` the bubble is placed for you, and a mash drained all 6 charges in one burst (lens:6, bubblePop). After that the fight is a slow slog of ping-off pellets, with 4 robots still near full hp at t90. The only thing a kid can find is "press V then shoot". It worked against every S1 enemy and the boss, whether or not the boss was weak to lightning. So it is one universal button, not a build. S1 ticks-to-kill (none / V / best targeted vent): brute 150 / 51 / 46 (frost); cinder 50 / 51 / -; sporelings x3 100 / 81 / 71 (pierce lens); mixed pack 105 / 91 / 91 (frost). Conductor wins or ties 3 of 4 fights, and I took 0 damage in all of them. Variety is thin. The puzzle is two things a kid never sees: which chamber is "next", and whether the bubble sits in the flight line. There is no rack UI, and bubbles look exactly like ordinary gems that auto-pick up. Mashing V destroys mods through the 2-cap. No phone or pad control exists, which is how the nephews actually play. Nobody would understand it without an adult, and they would get hurt by it without one. The whole slice needs one thing from the missing parts: a visible rack ring (LT-hold) that shows what vents, and pad and phone binds. It also needs a distinct bubble look with charge pips, a friendly-fire exception for casual mode, and the boss's weakness shown on screen (soundings or a swatch), so the "prep" is a choice and not a button. Toss and taps would add co-op talk, but only once the basics are legible. Keep Conductor; it is the one real thrill. Do not ship this to kids as it stands.

play A/kid.verdict: As the 10-year-old: I held both triggers and won everything, and I never learned what the goo does. S1 (seed 101) found no variety. The as-dealt hand (Striker SPARK/FLAME/FROST/IMPACT+pierce, Primer SOAK) won or tied all four fights, and each "smart" rebuild was slower. On the brute, the RIME+CRACK build killed at tick 154 and took 16 damage; mashing as dealt killed at 130 with no damage, the same tick as the Striker alone. The cinder died at tick 50 or 51 under every build. On the swarm, OIL+SPARK cleared at 101 against 60 as dealt, and the loss came from recharge and a fizzle. On the mixed pack, both triggers and the Striker alone cleared at the same ticks (40/60/100). The Primer's 0.9 splash without explosive rarely reaches more than one body, and 6-tile fights near a door never threatened the player. The reaction grammar works in the sim: the Magnet clump (hop reached 4), flash freeze into shatter, and steam blinding the boss are real. The weakness also matters: 138 against 240 ticks, and the neutral-boss control dropped to 52 hp. But the payoff for preparing is small next to the payoff for pressing the second trigger at all, since the Striker alone got downed by the weak boss. For the target audience, this slice cannot yet deliver. The Primer is keyboard `I` only, solo only, with no pad or touch button, so kids on controllers cannot fire it. Co-op does not carry the prime input or the coats. There is no bench and no what-will-execute strip, so the dual-face rule (lightning in the left gun becomes magnet) is invisible and reads as a bug. Four of five coats and every reaction have no on-screen feedback. Nothing tells you the boss is weak to lightning. To land, the missing parts must deliver five things: a pad trigger for the Primer; the bench with face-flip icons and a cast strip; visible coats plus callouts like "ARC x4!"; a boss dossier or reveal that surfaces the weakness; and harder rooms, so that mashing as dealt stops being the answer to everything. The reaction balance sweep also has to break that as-dealt dominance.

play A/planner.verdict: The grammar is the best-designed part of this: two triggers, coats that a verb consumes, and the Primer's cast order acting as a recipe (MAGNET then SOAK in one hold, then one Spark killed 5 thugs). That moment is a real "aha" and deserves to exist. As a build-crafting game, though, this slice does not yet deliver. One generic build, Soak+Spark, reached in two ejects with no cross-gun swap, won or tied every S1 fight and the boss. The as-dealt hand also beat everything with 0 damage, because STEAM (billed as a trap) blinds the target and trivialises melee enemies, and because enemies shot from beyond about 7 tiles never fight back. Tailoring for the lightning boss saved at most 30% of the ticks and cost 32 to 82 HP compared with the unprepared steam-control hand, so "prepare for the weak-to-lightning boss" is not yet a decision that matters. The weakness cannot be found in play either (only `look`'s resist field shows it). The reaction lookup table is small (4x4), and reaction damage is flat, so it ignores armour. The result is that arc is the universal answer and CRACK, IGNITE and FLASH FREEZE are side-grades. For a 10-year-old, holding both triggers produces reactions that depend on unseen flight times and 12-tick cast spacing, and walking over cartridges silently adds DUD casts to the Primer. For the design to deliver, the missing parts need to supply: (1) enemies that punish the generic answer, such as armour or resistances that scale reaction damage, a real counter to steam (bosses immune to blind), and wet-immune or insulated units, so a different enemy needs a different coat; (2) the bench and the what-will-execute HUD strip, so a kid sees 'MAGNET -> SOAK' before firing; (3) the boss dossier and banner, so the weakness is learned in play, plus a boss that can threaten a steam-kiter; (4) ground puddles and the spore cloud as soaked ground, which would make positioning part of the puzzle; (5) pad binding and co-op wire support, without which the nephews cannot play it at all today; (6) the section 10.3 balance sweep, run specifically against Soak+Spark dominance. It is a promising verb set that the current numbers and enemy roster collapse into a single build.

play B/kid.verdict: As the 10-year-old, I mashed attack with whatever wand I was handed and won every S1 fight on seed 101 without touching the order. The brute died by t=150 with me on 120/120 HP. The cinder died in 60 ticks at 120/120, even though fire was in the wand. The sporeling swarm was cleared by t=135 on 104 HP. The thug x2 + stalker pack routed by t=120 at 120/120. Rebuilding for the swarm (soak then shock) changed nothing: t=137 against t=135, and no chain fired, because sporelings never stand wet together. So variety is 1: one setup, the order you pick chips up in, wins everything. The reactions do fire (thermalCrack, shatter, numb, fizzle all show up in step replies), but they fire by accident from the default cycle, and a kid gets no signal that they happened. The slice has no reaction pops, no fizzle words, and no Dossier, so 'weak to lightning' and 'the boss is wet' exist only in `look` JSON. An adult would have to explain every one of FIZZLE, NUMB, primer, pocket, 'bare round', and 'only a bare round shatters'. Worse, the kid-obvious move of picking up a chip mid-fight drops it into the pocket, where it does nothing. The boss is where the mechanic almost works: one swap (Tesla first) took the wand-boss fight from a loss to a kill with 68 HP left. But a 3-tick timing change also flipped the unprepared run into a win, the 'smarter' prep (pocket the fizzling fire) did worse than the single swap, and on seed 202 the prepared run dealt less damage than the unprepared one. So prep matters less than whether the 5x shatter happens to land. The flashiest move in the PLAYBOOK, the area primer (eject soak, shoot it, chain the pack), wet nobody against the showcase's own drowners and cost me three times the damage. It can also soak you, and your own Tesla chain then zaps and stuns you, which is friendly fire in co-op. The missing parts are exactly what would make this readable to a kid. It needs on-screen reaction pops ('ZAP CHAIN!' and 'fizzle...'), a Dossier or a visible hide icon so the weakness is discoverable, pad controls for eject so the room half exists at all, and a faction filter on the chain. It also needs Twin/Trail/Relay or Steam/Wildfire so there is more than one good order. It needs enemies that cluster, or a bigger burst radius, so the pack-chain fantasy happens. Until then it is a lookup table played by accident, and the nephews would not notice it was there.

play C/planner.verdict: The slice has one great sentence: frost through a Storm lens freezes, arcs and shatters. It one-shots a 95 hp brute at t45 (versus t137 to t150 with a plain or reordered rack), and it is the only prep that turns the lightning-weak boss from a loss into a clean win (t180 kill for 22 damage, versus downed at t240). The weakness paying only when you set up ice is good design, and a planner can feel it: at electrified 1 the same play dies. Everything else is thin or broken. It is one pair reaction (Conductor), so the build question collapses to 'is there one big target? plant storm, shoot frost'. Against swarms and packs, every bubble play I tried was worse than doing nothing, because enemies walk into lenses and spend them as stun mines: sporelings 75 ticks and 0 damage plain, versus 165 ticks and 24 damage with a lens. The Flame mine does nothing to bodies at all. The puzzle content that exists is real but invisible: the first bubble crossed takes the rider, incendiary melts the Cold rider, a lens dies to the first enemy that touches it, a spent lens deletes the mod, and venting during a recharge restarts it. I only learned each rule by losing a boss fight and reading fx in the debug look. The owner could enjoy that as a lab. A 10-year-old cannot: bubbles render as the same mod gem kids already walk over to collect, walking over one does nothing, charges are not shown, and phone and pad players cannot vent at all, which excludes exactly the nephews this is for. Showcase fights (lens, lens-coop) are one firework burst (2 robots shattered by t20 to t31), then a 200+ tick grind with plain pellets once the 6 charges are gone. Soak→Tesla and Frost→Incendiary→Tesla are real ordered interactions, and one swap can change a brute opener from 13 damage to 65 damage in 45 ticks. As a slice, though, it does not deliver "different builds feel like different games." Across S1, [pierce] first (riding the next element) or [frost][incendiary] first was the best or tied answer against every enemy: brute 111 ticks, swarm 51, pack 121 (as loaded 100, within noise), cinder 31 via Crack, which bypasses its fire immunity. None of the four floor-1 fights ever threatened me (120/120 HP after most of them), so build choice did not matter for survival. Floor-1 fodder is too soft to ask the question. The area-primer puzzle is the most interesting idea, and in practice it is too fiddly. In the pack fight the thugs stood between me and my armed Soak chip, rounds hit them instead, and cracking it took 65 ticks. In wand-lab the burst wet 2 of the 4 drowners, and the only multi-body chain I got in the whole session hit 2 bodies (shock=2). Clearing the pack took longer than just shooting it as loaded. Lightning prep is shallow. The Mireclaw's hide makes shock chain whatever you do, so unprepared and prepared runs had the same boss HP curve through tick 168. Reordering was worth about 17% in kill time. Ejecting was a trap that killed me. The degenerate mono-shock wand deals 1.7x damage until the boss dries at half HP. Swap-chasing also lets the one Tesla chip fire several times per cycle, which defeats the copy cap. For a 10-year-old this is currently illegible. Fizzle and numb happen constantly and silently, the weakness exists only in debug output, and eject has no pad control. The missing parts need to deliver: (1) on-screen reaction pops, above all NUMB and FIZZLE, plus arrows on the HUD strip, without which none of this is learnable; (2) the Dossier, so the lightning weakness can be found in play; (3) something that makes a full wand beat a stripped one, such as a recharge that scales with fewer chips or a swap that costs recharge, plus a rule that a fired chip swapped back into the cursor does not refire; (4) Form chips (Twin, Trail, Relay) and an explosive chip in the S1 hand, so area primers do not depend on cracking floor chips through a crowd; (5) pad eject with a safety rule, since chips at your feet should not become self-traps; and (6) harder floors and tides where the wrong order actually loses the fight.
